Sohrawardî and the Platonists of Persia

Within the Islamic community, the Iranian world formed, from the very beginning, a distinct whole. Its character and calling can be understood only if we regard Iran's spiritual universe as one continuous whole, before Islam and after it. Islamic Iran has been, above all, the homeland of some of Islam's greatest philosophers and mystics.

For them, speculative thought can never be separated from the fruit it bears and its practical consequences—not in the social world, but in the whole, concrete spiritual reality that human beings nourish from their own substance beyond the boundaries of this life: their spiritual world.

The four-volume work in seven books presented here by Henry Corbin is the result of more than twenty years of research conducted in Iran itself. His method is fundamentally phenomenological, without belonging to any particular school. His aim is to encounter religious experience by allowing its object to appear just as it appears to those who experience it.

The phenomenologist must therefore become a spiritual guest of those to whom that religious reality reveals itself, and share with them the responsibility it brings. Any historical inquiry must remain within the terms of that reality rather than imposing foreign categories upon it from outside, whether dialectical or otherwise.

The first volume (Book I) sought to present some essential aspects of Twelver Shiism, or Imamism, which took root in Iran from the earliest times and became its official religion in the sixteenth century. This second volume (Book II) is devoted to the ishrâqîyûn, philosophers of illumination (from ishrâq, sunrise, the coming of light from the East), often described as “Platonists” in contrast with the Peripatetic philosophers of Islam.
At its origin stood the resolve of a brilliant young thinker, Sohrawardî, who died a martyr to his cause at the age of thirty-six (1191).

Through his writings he sought to revive the wisdom of ancient Persia, the philosophy of Light and Darkness, and to bring the Hellenized Magi home to Islamic Persia. He undertook this through the resources of spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) made available to him by Islamic spirituality.

We should recall once again that the word theosophy is used here in its original sense, from the Greek θεοσοφία, of which the Arabic hikmat ilâhîya is the literal equivalent. Sohrawardî understands it in the sense of ’irfân—knowledge that is gnosis. Rather than forming an abstract, conceptual picture of things, it involves direct perception (kashf), a real presence (hodûr, hozûr) of the spiritual worlds. ↩

Let us set out here, once and for all, which of Sohrawardî’s works have appeared in print to date. We have ourselves published two volumes, each with a substantial introductory study in French. The first is Opera metaphysica et mystica I (Bibliotheca Islamica, 16), Istanbul, 1945. It contains the metaphysical sections of three Arabic works forming a trilogy: Kitâb al-Talwîhât al-lawhîya wa’l-’arshîya, Kitâb al-Moqâwamât, and Kitâb al-Mashârî wa’l-Motârahât—respectively, The Book of Elucidations Inspired by the Tablet and the Throne, The Book of Resistances, and The Book of Crossroads and Conversations. The second volume, Œuvres philosophiques et mystiques I (= Opera metaphysica et mystica II), Tehran–Paris, 1952 (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 2), contains Kitâb Hikmat al-Ishrâq (The Book of Oriental Theosophy), Risâla fî i’tiqâd al-hokamâ’ (The Philosophers’ Profession of Faith), and Qissat al-ghorbat al-gharbîya (The Tale of the Western Exile, in Arabic and Persian). A third volume, Œuvres philosophiques et mystiques II (= Opera metaphysica et mystica III), contains the Works in Persian, edited by Seyyed Hosseïn Nasr, with a French introduction by H. Corbin (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 17), Tehran–Paris, 1969. This volume contains three major philosophical treatises, ten mystical epistles, and two further treatises whose authenticity, though highly probable, is not beyond doubt. Throughout this work we shall refer to these three volumes by the abbreviations Op. metaph. I, Op. metaph. II, and Op. metaph. III, and to their respective French introductory sections as Prolegomena I, II, and III. (While these notes were being written, we received a copy of the recent edition of Kitâb al-Lamahât [The Book of Lightning Glimpses], edited with introduction and notes by Emile Maalouf, Beirut, 1969.) ↩

Some historians are uncertain about the date of the shaykh al-Ishrâq’s death. The generally accepted date is 587 AH, although Shahrazôrî hesitates between the end of 586 and 588 AH. ’Imâd al-Dîn (above, p. 15, n. 11) places the account under the year 588. Abû’l-Fedâ confirms 587 AH (Recueil des historiens des croisades. Historiens orientaux, vol. I, Paris, 1872, p. 65). Let us also mention two works from our youth: (1) Sohrawardî d’Alep, fondateur de la doctrine illuminative (ishrâqî) [Publications de la Société des Études iraniennes, no. 16], Paris, 1939; and (2) Les motifs zoroastriens dans la philosophie de Sohrawardî (Publications de la Société d’iranologie, no. 3), Tehran, 1946. The first of these titles contains two inaccuracies, excusable perhaps by youthful inexperience and the example set by our elders. “Sohrawardî of Aleppo” is misleading: someone who comes from Sohraward cannot also be a native of Aleppo. The designation (nisba) al-Halabî, found in some historians, means here not “from Aleppo” but “who died in Aleppo.” Second, we had used the word “illuminative” to translate ishrâqî. One need only consult the texts we have published since then, our Prolegomena (above, p. 12, n. 3), and the discussions later in this book to see that Sohrawardî’s intention was indeed to establish an “Oriental” (ishrâqî) theosophy, giving “Orient” the meaning he himself assigns to it. It should therefore be clearly understood that the shaykh al-Ishrâq, or sâhib al-Ishrâq, is the “master of Oriental theosophy,” and that he came from Sohraward in Iran (in the province of Jabal, ancient Media). Shahrazôrî has also preserved some vivid details about his appearance and habits: he was perfectly proportioned in height and build; his hair and beard were reddish-blond; he enjoyed samâ’, gatherings for music; he scorned the outward marks of authority and worldly vanity. Sometimes he wore a long, flowing robe and a richly coloured headdress; at other times he dressed in patched garments, or simply wore the Sufis’ woollen clothing. ↩

Jâmâsp was a disciple of Zoroaster and married his daughter Pouruchtishta. See H. S. Nyberg, Die Religionen des alten Irans, Leipzig, 1938, pp. 151 ff., where Yasna 53 is interpreted as a “marriage liturgy.” He is said to have committed the Avesta to writing (A. V. W. Jackson, Zoroaster, the Prophet of Ancient Iran, New York, 1938, p. 117, n. 3, referring to the Dênkard), and was Zoroaster’s first successor in the priestly office. A considerable body of literature, chiefly astrological and apocalyptic, bears his name; see Bidez and Cumont, Les Mages hellénisés, index under Djâmâspa and Zâmâsp-Nâmak. It has yet to receive a systematic study. ↩

Frashaoshtra was Jâmâsp’s brother and became Zoroaster’s father-in-law when Zoroaster married his daughter Hvôvi as his third wife. Frashaoshtra and Jâmâsp were members of the court of Vishtaspa, the ruler who supported Zoroaster’s preaching. Hvôvi remains a sacred figure of the end times: her children, the three Saoshyants or Saviours, whose successive arrivals will bring our Aeon to a close, have not yet been born. See H. S. Nyberg, op. cit., index under Hvôgva-Geschlecht and Frashaoshtra. ↩

Bozorgmehr was chief physician and minister to the Sasanian ruler Khosrow Anûshirvân (= Khosrow “of the immortal soul,” d. 579 CE). His figure is linked with the legend of Ahikar, and therefore with the Book of Tobit, as well as with the introduction of chess into Persia. He was probably none other than the celebrated physician Burzoë, translator of Kalîlagh and Damnag into Pahlavi. See A.
